about: Process Analysis (CENG40002) is a 5-credit core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, taught in the Autumn term. No public module descriptor was found, so this pack covers the standard first-year process analysis syllabus of material and energy balances on single and multi-unit, reactive and non-reactive processes; the programme's learning outcomes name process analysis as a core area, but the topic list here is this pack's own. The programme specification gives assessment only at programme level, so check the module's own assessment details at the start of term.
topics: The general balance equation and degree-of-freedom analysis
Material balances on non-reactive single units
Multi-unit processes: recycle, bypass and purge
Reactive systems: extent, conversion, yield and selectivity

notes.body:
Every process analysis problem starts with describing the streams correctly. Most marks lost in first-year balance questions come from muddled units or from mixing up mass and mole fractions, not from difficult maths.

Amounts and flows
- Mass m (kg) and amount of substance n (mol or kmol) are linked by the molar mass M: n = m/M. Working in kmol and kg/kmol keeps numbers tidy.
- Flow rates: mass flow ṁ (kg/s), molar flow ṅ (kmol/h) and volumetric flow Q̇ (m³/s), with Q̇ = ṁ/ρ.
- Mass fraction w_i = m_i/Σm and mole fraction x_i = n_i/Σn. Each set sums to 1, which is itself an equation you can use.
- Average molar mass of a mixture: M̄ = Σ x_i M_i (from mole fractions) or M̄ = 1/Σ(w_i/M_i) (from mass fractions).

Worked example: mass to mole fractions
A stream is 40 wt% ethanol (M ≈ 46.07 kg/kmol) and 60 wt% water (M ≈ 18.02 kg/kmol). Take a basis of 100 kg.
- Ethanol: 40/46.07 = 0.868 kmol; water: 60/18.02 = 3.330 kmol.
- x_ethanol = 0.868/(0.868 + 3.330) = 0.207.
- M̄ = 100 kg / 4.198 kmol = 23.8 kg/kmol.
Notice that 40 wt% is only about 21 mol%: the light water molecules dominate on a mole basis.

Pressure and temperature
- Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar.
- T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15. A temperature difference has the same size in K and °C, so a heat capacity in kJ/kg K can be used with a ΔT in °C.
- Ideal gas law: PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/mol K. At 0 °C and 1 atm one mole of ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L; be careful, because different industries define "standard conditions" differently.

Basis of calculation
Choose a basis (for example 100 mol of feed, or 1 hour of operation) when no flow is given, or when a convenient amount makes the arithmetic easier. Because balances without reaction rates are linear in the flows, the answers can be scaled to the real flow at the end.

Dimensional homogeneity
Every term added or equated must have the same units. Arguments of exp and ln must be dimensionless. Checking units at each line is the fastest way to catch slips such as kJ against kW or kmol/h against mol/s.

Flowsheets
Draw a box for each unit and an arrow for each stream, and label every stream with its total flow and its composition, writing unknowns as symbols (ṅ₃, x₃,A). A fully labelled flowsheet is the starting point for the degree-of-freedom count in the next topic and is usually worth marks in its own right.

Exam tips: state your basis, convert all compositions to one basis (mass or mole) before writing balances, and carry units on every number.

notes.h: The general balance equation and degree-of-freedom analysis
notes.body:
The general balance
For any quantity (total mass, a species, energy) and any chosen system boundary:

Input + Generation − Output − Consumption = Accumulation

- Steady state: nothing changes with time, so Accumulation = 0.
- Non-reactive species: Generation = Consumption = 0, so for a steady process Input = Output for each species.
- Total mass is conserved even with reaction (chemical processes do not convert mass to energy in any measurable way), but total moles are not, because reactions can change the number of molecules (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ turns 4 mol into 2 mol).
- Atoms of each element are conserved in chemical reactions, so element balances are always of the simple In = Out form at steady state.

Differential and integral balances
- A differential balance is written in terms of rates (kg/s, kmol/h) and applies to continuous processes at an instant.
- An integral balance is written in terms of amounts (kg, kmol) between two times; it suits batch processes, where Initial input + Generation = Final output + Consumption.

Independent equations
For a non-reactive process involving S species you can write S independent material balances: either one per species, or S − 1 species balances plus the total balance. Writing all S species balances and the total gives S + 1 equations but only S are independent, a common way to get a false degree-of-freedom count. A splitter is special: all outlets have the inlet composition, so only one independent material balance (the total) can be written, and the remaining relations are composition restrictions.

Degree-of-freedom (DOF) analysis
DOF = number of unknowns − number of independent equations.

The equations include material balances, energy balances, stated specifications (e.g. "90% recovery"), physical relations (phase equilibrium, density) and, if fractions are unknowns, the requirement that fractions sum to 1.
- DOF = 0: the problem is specified and can be solved.
- DOF > 0: under-specified; more information is needed (or the extra freedom is a design variable to optimise).
- DOF < 0: over-specified; the data are redundant and possibly inconsistent.
For reactive systems, each independent reaction adds one unknown extent ξ but every species balance gains a generation term, so the bookkeeping is: unknowns + extents − (species balances + other relations).

Worked example: a mixer
Stream 1 (unknown ṁ₁) is pure A. Stream 2 is 100 kg/h with 20 wt% A. The outlet has 50 wt% A and unknown flow ṁ₃.
- Unknowns: ṁ₁, ṁ₃ (2). Independent balances: 2 (A and total). DOF = 0.
- Total: ṁ₁ + 100 = ṁ₃. A: ṁ₁ + 20 = 0.5ṁ₃.
- Substituting: ṁ₁ + 20 = 0.5ṁ₁ + 50, so ṁ₁ = 60 kg/h and ṁ₃ = 160 kg/h. Check: A out = 80 = 60 + 20.

Multi-unit systems
Do a DOF count for each unit, for any mixing or splitting points, and for the overall process. Start with whichever subsystem has DOF = 0, then use the solved streams to reduce the DOF of the neighbours.

Exam tips: always write the DOF table before solving; examiners at first-year level reward the count itself, and it stops you chasing an unsolvable problem.

notes.h: Material balances on non-reactive single units
notes.body:
A reliable routine
1. Draw and fully label the flowsheet.
2. Choose a basis if no flow is given.
3. Convert compositions to a single basis (all mass or all mole).
4. Do the DOF count.
5. Write balances, starting with any equation that contains only one unknown.
6. Solve, then check with a balance you did not use.

Tie components
A tie component passes from one stream to another unchanged (for example the dissolved solids in an evaporator or the dry solid in a dryer). A balance on it often gives an unknown flow directly.

Example 1: evaporator
1000 kg/h of a 10 wt% sugar solution is concentrated to 50 wt%.
- Sugar (tie component): 0.10 × 1000 = 0.50 × P, so P = 200 kg/h.
- Total: 1000 = P + W, so water evaporated W = 800 kg/h.
Note that the product still contains 100 kg/h of water, which is why W is not 900 kg/h.

Example 2: dryer
100 kg of wet solid with 40 wt% water is dried to 10 wt% water.
- Dry solid: 60 kg in, and it makes up 90% of the product, so product = 60/0.9 = 66.7 kg.
- Water removed = 100 − 66.7 = 33.3 kg. Subtracting percentages (40 − 10 = 30 kg) is wrong because the product mass is smaller than the feed.

Example 3: binary distillation split
A column receives 100 kmol/h of a feed with 40 mol% benzene. The distillate is 95 mol% benzene and the bottoms 5 mol% benzene.
- Total: 100 = D + B.
- Benzene: 40 = 0.95D + 0.05B.
- Solving: D = 100(0.40 − 0.05)/(0.95 − 0.05) = 38.9 kmol/h and B = 61.1 kmol/h.
- Fractional recovery of benzene in the distillate = 0.95 × 38.9/40 = 0.924 (92.4%).
The general form D/F = (z − x_B)/(x_D − x_B) is the lever rule: the feed composition lies between the two product compositions, and the flows are inversely proportional to the distances.

Specifications you will meet
- Fractional recovery: the fraction of a species in the feed that leaves in a named product.
- Split fraction: the fraction of a whole stream sent one way at a splitter.
- Purity: the composition of a product.
Recoveries and purities are not interchangeable: a column can give a very pure distillate while recovering only a small fraction of the light component.

Scaling
If a balance is solved on a basis of 100 kmol and the real feed is 250 kmol/h, multiply every flow by 2.5; compositions do not change.

Exam tips: identify the tie component first, write the lever-rule result as a quick check, and always confirm with an unused balance.

notes.h: Multi-unit processes: recycle, bypass and purge
notes.body:
Real plants link several units. Three stream structures appear constantly in first-year problems.

Recycle
Part of a product stream is returned to an earlier point, usually to send unreacted feed back to a reactor or to recover a valuable solvent. Recycle lets a process achieve a high overall conversion even when the reactor converts only a fraction per pass, for example because of equilibrium or selectivity limits.

Two conversions must be kept distinct:
- Single-pass conversion = (reactant entering reactor − reactant leaving reactor)/reactant entering reactor.
- Overall conversion = (reactant in fresh feed − reactant leaving the whole process)/reactant in fresh feed.

Worked example: recycle with perfect separation
100 mol/h of A is fed. The reactor converts 25% of the A entering it, and a separator returns all unreacted A.
- Overall: all A eventually reacts, so 100 mol/h reacts.
- Reactor: 0.25 × (reactor feed) = 100, so reactor feed = 400 mol/h.
- Recycle = 400 − 100 = 300 mol/h; recycle ratio (recycle/fresh feed) = 3.

Purge
If the fresh feed contains an inert or impurity that the separator cannot remove, it would build up in a recycle loop without limit. A purge bleeds off a small fraction of the recycle so that the inert leaves at the same rate it enters. The price is that some valuable reactant is lost with the purge, so overall conversion falls below 100%.

Worked example: purge
Fresh feed: 100 mol/h with 99 mol% A and 1 mol% inert I. Single-pass conversion of A is 20%. All product is removed; unreacted A and all the I go to a splitter, and the purge composition is limited to 10 mol% I.
- Overall I balance: 1 = 0.10P, so P = 10 mol/h, carrying 9 mol/h of A.
- Overall A: 99 = reacted + 9, so 90 mol/h reacts. Overall conversion = 90/99 = 90.9%.
- Reactor: A entering = 90/0.20 = 450 mol/h; A leaving = 360 mol/h.
- Splitter inlet = 360/0.9 = 400 mol/h, so recycle R = 400 − 10 = 390 mol/h.
- Check at the mixer: 99 + 0.9 × 390 = 450 mol/h of A.

Bypass
Part of a feed goes round a unit and rejoins the product. It is used to hit a product specification exactly or to reduce the load on the unit. Treat the splitting point, the unit and the mixing point as separate subsystems.

Solution strategy
- Start with the overall balance: internal streams such as recycle cancel, and the DOF is often zero.
- Then balance a mixing point, a splitter or a single unit whose DOF has become zero.
- In process simulators, recycle loops are solved iteratively by guessing a "tear stream" and repeating until it converges; by hand, simultaneous linear equations do the same job.

Exam tips: state which conversion you are using, and remember the overall balance boundary cuts only fresh feed, product and purge streams.

notes.h: Reactive systems: extent, conversion, yield and selectivity
notes.body:
Stoichiometry
In a balanced equation, stoichiometric coefficients ν_i are negative for reactants and positive for products. For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: ν_N₂ = −1, ν_H₂ = −3, ν_NH₃ = +2.

Extent of reaction
For a single reaction the outlet amount of every species follows from one number, the extent ξ (mol or mol/s):
n_i = n_i0 + ν_i ξ
Because ξ is the same for every species, it is the cleanest way to write reactive balances. With several independent reactions, n_i = n_i0 + Σ_j ν_ij ξ_j.

Limiting and excess reactants
- The limiting reactant is the one that would run out first if the reaction went to completion: the smallest n_i0/|ν_i|.
- Fractional excess of a reactant = (amount fed − amount needed to react with all the limiting reactant)/amount needed.

Worked example: ammonia
Feed: 100 mol N₂ and 250 mol H₂.
- H₂: 250/3 = 83.3; N₂: 100/1 = 100. H₂ gives the smaller value, so H₂ is limiting.
- N₂ needed for 250 mol H₂ = 83.3 mol; excess = (100 − 83.3)/83.3 = 20%.
- If 60% of the H₂ reacts: ξ = 0.6 × 250/3 = 50 mol. Outlet: N₂ = 100 − 50 = 50 mol; H₂ = 250 − 150 = 100 mol; NH₃ = 0 + 100 = 100 mol. Total moles fall from 350 to 250, as expected.

Conversion
Fractional conversion of A: f_A = (n_A0 − n_A)/n_A0. Conversion can be limited by equilibrium (as in ammonia synthesis) rather than stoichiometry, so 100% conversion is not guaranteed even with excess co-reactant.

Multiple reactions: yield and selectivity
When a reactant can form a desired and an undesired product, two extra measures appear. Textbooks define them in more than one way, so always state your definition.
- Yield (based on feed) = moles of desired product formed / moles of reactant fed (adjusted for stoichiometry if needed).
- Yield (based on consumption) = moles of desired product formed / moles of reactant consumed.
- Selectivity = moles of desired product / moles of undesired product.

Worked example: ethylene oxidation
C₂H₄ + ½O₂ → C₂H₄O (desired); C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O (undesired).
100 mol C₂H₄ is fed; the outlet contains 20 mol C₂H₄ and 56 mol C₂H₄O.
- C₂H₄ consumed = 80 mol, so conversion = 80%.
- ξ₁ = 56 mol; ξ₂ = 80 − 56 = 24 mol, producing 48 mol CO₂ and 48 mol H₂O, and using 28 + 72 = 100 mol O₂.
- Yield on feed = 56/100 = 0.56; yield on consumption = 56/80 = 0.70.
- Selectivity (ethylene oxide per ethylene burned) = 56/24 = 2.33.

Exam tips: tabulate in, change (ν_i ξ) and out for each species; the table makes DOF and checks obvious.

Combustion problems are reactive balances with their own vocabulary, and they appear in almost every process analysis exam.

Air
For balances, air is usually taken as 21 mol% O₂ and 79 mol% N₂ (argon and other minor gases lumped with N₂), so each mole of O₂ brings 79/21 = 3.76 mol of N₂.

Theoretical oxygen and excess air
- Theoretical O₂ is the amount needed to burn all the fuel completely: carbon to CO₂, hydrogen to H₂O, sulfur to SO₂.
- Theoretical air = theoretical O₂/0.21.
- Percentage excess air = (air fed − theoretical air)/theoretical air × 100, which equals the same percentage for O₂.
- Theoretical oxygen is defined assuming complete combustion even if, in practice, some CO forms. A common error is to recompute it from the actual products.

Wet and dry basis
A flue gas analysis on a dry basis excludes water. Traditional Orsat-type analysers report dry compositions because the sample is cooled and the water condenses. Convert by dividing each species by the dry total.

Worked example: methane with 20% excess air
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, burning 100 mol/h CH₄ completely.
- Theoretical O₂ = 200 mol/h; O₂ fed = 1.2 × 200 = 240 mol/h.
- Air fed = 240/0.21 = 1143 mol/h; N₂ = 0.79 × 1143 = 903 mol/h.
- Flue gas: CO₂ 100, H₂O 200, O₂ 240 − 200 = 40, N₂ 903 mol/h. Wet total = 1243 mol/h.
- Dry total = 1043 mol/h. Dry composition: CO₂ 9.6%, O₂ 3.8%, N₂ 86.6%.
- On a wet basis CO₂ is only 8.0%, so always say which basis you quote.

Element (atom) balances
For complex or unknown reactions, balance atoms instead of molecules. At steady state, atoms in = atoms out for each element, with no generation term. Typical uses:
- Finding the composition of a fuel from a dry flue gas analysis: a carbon balance links fuel to CO₂ (and CO); an N₂ balance gives the air fed; an oxygen balance then gives the water formed and hence the hydrogen in the fuel.
- Checking a reactive balance done with extents.
The number of independent element balances can be less than the number of elements if some always appear in fixed ratios.

Incomplete combustion
With too little air or poor mixing, CO forms. Since CO formation releases much less energy than burning carbon to CO₂ and CO is toxic, combustion equipment runs with modest excess air. Too much excess air, though, wastes energy heating the extra N₂.

Exam tips: compute theoretical O₂ from the fuel first, write N₂ = 3.76 × O₂ fed, and quote flue gas compositions on the basis requested.

Forms of energy
- Kinetic energy E_k = ½mu².
- Potential energy E_p = mgz.
- Internal energy U: the molecular energy of the material.
- Enthalpy H = U + PV, which conveniently bundles the internal energy with the flow work needed to push material in and out of an open system.

Heat Q is energy crossing the boundary because of a temperature difference; work W is energy crossing for any other reason (shafts, moving boundaries, electricity). Neither is a property of the system: they depend on the path. U and H are state functions.

The first law
- Closed system: Q − W = ΔU + ΔE_k + ΔE_p, with W the work done by the system (sign conventions differ between texts, so state yours).
- Open system at steady state (steady-flow energy equation): Q̇ − Ẇ_s = ΔḢ + ΔĖ_k + ΔĖ_p, where ΔḢ = Σ outlet ṁĤ − Σ inlet ṁĤ and Ẇ_s is shaft work.
For most heaters, coolers, mixers and reactors the kinetic and potential terms are negligible and the balance reduces to Q̇ = ΔḢ.

Calculating enthalpy changes
Enthalpy is relative to a reference state, so choose one for each species (for example liquid water at 25 °C) and use it consistently. Then build a path:
- Sensible heat: ΔĤ = ∫c_p dT ≈ c_p ΔT for modest ranges. For liquid water, c_p ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg K (approximate).
- Latent heat for phase changes: for water at 100 °C, ΔĤ_vap ≈ 2257 kJ/kg (approximate; it falls as pressure and temperature rise).
- Steam tables give Ĥ directly for water and steam and avoid errors from assuming constant c_p.
Because H is a state function, any convenient hypothetical path between the same end states gives the same ΔH.

Worked example: steam heater
1000 kg/h of water is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by saturated steam that condenses and leaves as saturated liquid (take the latent heat as 2200 kJ/kg).
- Q̇ = ṁc_pΔT = (1000/3600) × 4.18 × 60 = 69.7 kW.
- Steam = 69.7/2200 = 0.0317 kg/s = 114 kg/h.

Worked example: adiabatic mixing
2 kg/s of water at 80 °C mixes with 3 kg/s at 20 °C. With Q̇ = 0 and constant c_p, the outlet temperature is the mass-weighted mean: T = (2 × 80 + 3 × 20)/5 = 44 °C.

Mechanical energy balance
For incompressible liquids with no heat effects, the energy balance becomes a mechanical energy (extended Bernoulli) balance: ΔP/ρ + Δu²/2 + gΔz + friction losses = shaft work input per kg. It is used to size pumps and is developed further in fluid mechanics.

Exam tips: state the reference states, list each term in the energy balance and say which you neglect and why.

Heat of reaction
The standard heat of reaction ΔĤ_r° is the enthalpy change when stoichiometric amounts of reactants at a standard state (usually 25 °C and 1 bar or 1 atm) react completely to products at the same state. It is negative for exothermic reactions. Its value depends on the phases, so always specify, for example, H₂O(l) or H₂O(g).

Heats of formation and Hess's law
- ΔĤ_f° is the enthalpy change for forming 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states; for an element in its standard state it is zero.
- Hess's law: because enthalpy is a state function, ΔĤ_r° = Σ ν_i ΔĤ_f,i° (products positive, reactants negative).

Worked example: methane combustion
Approximate standard heats of formation (kJ/mol): CH₄ −74.8; CO₂ −393.5; H₂O(g) −241.8; H₂O(l) −285.8.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
- With water vapour: ΔĤ_r° = −393.5 + 2(−241.8) − (−74.8) = −802.3 kJ/mol.
- With liquid water: −393.5 + 2(−285.8) + 74.8 = −890.3 kJ/mol.
- The difference (88.0 kJ/mol) is twice the latent heat of water at 25 °C (≈ 44.0 kJ/mol).
These correspond to the lower and higher heating values: the higher heating value assumes the product water is condensed, so it is larger.

Two ways to write the balance
1. Heat of reaction method (convenient for a single known reaction): take reactants and products at 25 °C as references, then
   ΔḢ = ξΔĤ_r° + Σ outlet ṅ_iĤ_i − Σ inlet ṅ_iĤ_i,
   where each Ĥ_i is the sensible (and latent) enthalpy from 25 °C to the stream condition.
2. Heat of formation method (convenient for multiple reactions): take the elements at 25 °C as the reference, so each species' enthalpy is ΔĤ_f° plus its sensible enthalpy, and ΔḢ = Σ out ṅĤ − Σ in ṅĤ. No extents are needed.

Adiabatic flame temperature
If combustion is adiabatic (Q̇ = 0) with no shaft work, the heat released heats the products:
−ξΔĤ_r° = Σ ṅ_i c̄_p,i (T_ad − 25 °C)
using mean heat capacities. Excess air lowers T_ad because more gas must be heated. Simple constant-c_p estimates overpredict the real value because heat capacities rise with temperature and products dissociate at high temperature; the adiabatic flame temperature of methane in stoichiometric air is about 1950 °C (approximate).

Worked example: heat removal
10 mol/s of methane burns completely with feed and products both at 25 °C and water leaving as vapour. Q̇ = ξΔĤ_r° = 10 × (−802.3) = −8023 kW: about 8.0 MW must be removed.

Exam tips: write the reaction with phases, show ΔĤ_r° from formation data with signs, and say whether you use the heat of reaction or heat of formation method.

cards.b: x_i = n_i/Σn: moles of species i divided by total moles in the stream. Mole fractions of all species sum to 1.

cards.f: Converting mass fractions to mole fractions
cards.b: Take a basis (e.g. 100 kg), divide each species' mass by its molar mass to get moles, then divide each by the total moles.

cards.f: Average molar mass from mass fractions
cards.b: M̄ = 1/Σ(w_i/M_i). From mole fractions it is M̄ = Σ x_i M_i.
P_abs = P_gauge + P_atm. Gas laws and vapour pressure relations need absolute pressure.
A chosen amount or flow (e.g. 100 mol feed or 1 h) on which a balance is solved; results scale linearly to the real flow when no rate laws are involved.
Every term in an equation must have the same units; arguments of exp, ln and similar functions must be dimensionless.
About 22.4 L/mol (0.0224 m³/mol) at 0 °C and 1 atm, from V/n = RT/P. Other 'standard' conditions give different values.
Input + Generation − Output − Consumption = Accumulation, written for total mass, a species, atoms or energy over a defined system.
No property of the system changes with time, so the accumulation term is zero.
Number of unknowns minus number of independent equations. DOF = 0: solvable; DOF > 0: under-specified; DOF < 0: over-specified (redundant, possibly inconsistent).

cards.f: Independent material balances, non-reactive, S species
cards.b: S: either S species balances or S − 1 species balances plus the total. The total and all S species balances are not independent.
All outlets of a splitter have the inlet composition, so only one independent material balance (total) is available; the rest are composition restrictions.

cards.f: Is total moles conserved in a reactor?
cards.b: No. Total mass and atoms of each element are conserved, but reactions can change the number of molecules, so total moles can rise or fall.
Differential: rates at an instant (continuous processes). Integral: amounts between two times (batch processes).

cards.f: Extra unknowns in a reactive DOF count
cards.b: One extent of reaction per independent reaction (or, equivalently, use element balances instead of species balances).
A material that passes from one stream to another unchanged (e.g. dry solid through a dryer); a balance on it often gives a flow directly.
Fraction of a species in the feed that leaves in a specified product stream, e.g. D x_D/(F z) for the light component in the distillate.

cards.f: Lever rule for a binary split
cards.b: D/F = (z − x_B)/(x_D − x_B) and B/F = (x_D − z)/(x_D − x_B): flows are inversely proportional to the composition distances from the feed.

cards.f: Evaporator: 1000 kg/h at 10 wt% solids → 50 wt%
cards.b: Solids balance: 100 = 0.5P so P = 200 kg/h; water evaporated = 800 kg/h.

cards.f: Why check with an unused balance?
cards.b: It catches arithmetic and set-up slips: a correct solution satisfies every independent and dependent balance.
Purity is the composition of a product; recovery is the fraction of a feed component captured in it. High purity does not imply high recovery.
(reactant into reactor − reactant out of reactor)/reactant into reactor.
(reactant in fresh feed − reactant leaving the whole process)/reactant in fresh feed.
To return unreacted feed or valuable material so overall conversion or recovery is high even when single-pass conversion is limited.
To stop inerts or impurities accumulating in a recycle loop: it removes them at the rate they enter, at the cost of losing some reactant.
Part of a feed is routed round a unit and remixed with its outlet, often to meet a product specification exactly.

cards.f: First balance to try on a recycle problem
cards.b: The overall balance: recycle streams are internal and cancel, so it usually has the fewest unknowns.
Recycle flow divided by fresh feed flow (definitions vary; some texts use recycle/reactor feed, so state yours).
A recycle stream whose values are guessed and iterated in sequential-modular simulation until the guessed and calculated values agree.
Defined by n_i = n_i0 + ν_i ξ for every species in a single reaction; ν_i negative for reactants, positive for products.
The reactant with the smallest n_i0/|ν_i|: the one that would be used up first if the reaction went to completion.
(amount fed − stoichiometric amount needed for the limiting reactant)/stoichiometric amount needed.
f_A = (n_A0 − n_A)/n_A0: the fraction of A fed that reacts.
Desired product formed per reactant fed (or per reactant consumed). Definitions vary, so state which you use.
Moles of desired product formed per mole of undesired product formed (one common definition).

cards.f: Why might conversion stay below 100% even with excess co-reactant?
cards.b: The reaction may be equilibrium-limited, or kinetics may be too slow for the residence time.
O₂ needed for complete combustion of the fuel fed (C→CO₂, H→H₂O, S→SO₂), whether or not combustion is actually complete.
(air fed − theoretical air)/theoretical air × 100; equal to the percentage excess O₂.

cards.f: N₂ accompanying 1 mol O₂ in air
cards.b: 79/21 ≈ 3.76 mol, using the usual 21/79 approximation for air.
Composition with water excluded; each species divided by the total moles of non-water gas.
Atoms in = atoms out for each element at steady state, with no generation or consumption terms. Useful when reactions are unknown.

cards.f: Methane with 20% excess air: dry CO₂ fraction
cards.b: Per 100 mol CH₄: CO₂ 100, O₂ 40, N₂ 903; dry total 1043, so CO₂ ≈ 9.6 mol% dry (8.0% wet).

cards.f: Why not use a huge excess of air?
cards.b: The extra N₂ and O₂ must be heated, lowering flame temperature and efficiency; too little air gives CO and unburnt fuel.
Q̇ − Ẇ_s = ΔḢ + ΔĖ_k + ΔĖ_p for an open system at steady state (Ẇ_s = shaft work done by the system).
H = U + PV, a state function combining internal energy and flow work; only changes in H are meaningful, relative to a chosen reference state.
ΔĤ = ∫c_p dT, approximately c_p ΔT if c_p is roughly constant over the range.
About 4.18 kJ/kg K (75.3 J/mol K) near room temperature.

cards.f: Latent heat of vaporisation of water at 100 °C (approx.)
cards.b: About 2257 kJ/kg (≈ 40.7 kJ/mol); smaller at higher saturation temperatures.

cards.f: Adiabatic mixing of two water streams
cards.b: With constant c_p the outlet temperature is the mass-flow-weighted mean, e.g. 2 kg/s at 80 °C + 3 kg/s at 20 °C → 44 °C.

cards.f: Why can a hypothetical path be used to find ΔH?
cards.b: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route.
Enthalpy change when stoichiometric reactants at the standard state react fully to products at the same state; negative if exothermic.
ΔĤ_r° = Σ ν_i ΔĤ_f,i°: because H is a state function, reaction enthalpies can be built from formation enthalpies.

cards.f: Heat of formation of an element in its standard state
cards.b: Zero by definition (e.g. O₂(g), N₂(g), C(graphite) at 25 °C).
HHV assumes product water is liquid; LHV assumes it is vapour. HHV is larger by the latent heat of the water formed.
About −802 kJ/mol CH₄ (about −890 kJ/mol if the water is liquid).
Product temperature when combustion occurs with no heat loss or work: heat released = sensible heat taken up by the products.
Uses elements at 25 °C as reference so each species' enthalpy includes ΔĤ_f°; handles multiple reactions without extents.

cards.f: Effect of excess air on adiabatic flame temperature
cards.b: It lowers it: the same heat is shared among more moles of gas.

questions.q: A solution is 50 wt% methanol (M ≈ 32.04 kg/kmol) and 50 wt% water (M ≈ 18.02 kg/kmol). What is the mole fraction of methanol?
questions.why: On a 100 kg basis there are 50/32.04 = 1.56 kmol of methanol and 50/18.02 = 2.77 kmol of water, so x = 1.56/4.33 = 0.360. The value 0.500 is the mass fraction, which is not the same as the mole fraction when molar masses differ. 0.640 is the mole fraction of water, not methanol. 0.562 is the mole ratio of methanol to water (1.56/2.77), which divides by water moles only instead of by total moles.

questions.q: A stream is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. What is the temperature rise expressed in kelvin?
questions.why: Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, so a difference of 30 °C is a difference of 30 K. 303.15 K is what you get by adding 273.15 to the difference, but the offset only applies to absolute temperatures, not differences. 54 K comes from multiplying by 1.8, the factor for Fahrenheit or Rankine degrees. 323.15 K is the final temperature (50 °C) converted to kelvin, not the rise.

questions.q: A flue gas contains 20 mol% CO₂ (M ≈ 44.01 kg/kmol) and 80 mol% N₂ (M ≈ 28.01 kg/kmol). (a) Find the mass fraction of CO₂ and the average molar mass. (b) Estimate the gas density at 1 atm and 25 °C assuming ideal-gas behaviour.
markScheme: Basis stated (e.g. 100 mol) and masses found: CO₂ 880.2 g, N₂ 2240.8 g (1 mark)
ρ = PM̄/RT used with consistent SI units (1 mark)

questions.q: In a continuous reactor at steady state, which of the following is NOT necessarily conserved between inlet and outlet?
questions.why: Reactions rearrange atoms into different molecules, and the number of molecules can change (for example 1 mol of N₂ and 3 mol of H₂, 4 mol in all, give 2 mol of NH₃), so total moles need not balance. Total mass is conserved in chemical reactions. Atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so both the moles and the mass of each element are conserved at steady state.

questions.q: A non-reactive unit has three species. Its three streams contain four unknown quantities in total and no other specifications or relations are given. What is the degree of freedom?
questions.why: Three species give three independent material balances, so DOF = 4 − 3 = 1 and the problem is under-specified. A DOF of 0 results from counting the total balance as a fourth independent equation, but it is just the sum of the three species balances. 4 is the number of unknowns with no equations subtracted. 3 is the number of independent balances, not the DOF.

questions.q: Stream 1 (pure A, unknown flow) mixes with Stream 2 (100 kg/h, 20 wt% A, rest B) to give a product of 50 wt% A. Carry out a degree-of-freedom analysis and find both unknown flows.
markScheme: Unknowns identified as ṁ₁ and ṁ₃ and two independent balances, so DOF = 0 (1 mark)
Total balance ṁ₁ + 100 = ṁ₃ (1 mark)
A balance ṁ₁ + 20 = 0.5ṁ₃ (1 mark)
ṁ₁ = 60 kg/h, ṁ₃ = 160 kg/h, with a check (e.g. B: 80 = 0.5 × 160) (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Unknowns: ṁ₁ and ṁ₃. Two species give two independent balances, and no other relations are needed, so DOF = 2 − 2 = 0. Total: ṁ₁ + 100 = ṁ₃. A: ṁ₁ + 0.2 × 100 = 0.5ṁ₃. Substituting the total balance: ṁ₁ + 20 = 0.5ṁ₁ + 50, so ṁ₁ = 60 kg/h and ṁ₃ = 160 kg/h. Check with B: in = 80 kg/h; out = 0.5 × 160 = 80 kg/h.

questions.q: 1000 kg/h of a 10 wt% sugar solution is concentrated to 50 wt% sugar in an evaporator. How much water is evaporated?
questions.why: A sugar balance gives 100 = 0.5P, so the product is 200 kg/h and the water evaporated is 1000 − 200 = 800 kg/h. 200 kg/h is the concentrated product flow, not the vapour. 400 kg/h comes from multiplying the feed by the difference in percentages (50 − 10 = 40%), which is not a balance on anything. 900 kg/h is all the water in the feed, but the product still contains 100 kg/h of water.

questions.q: 100 kg of wet solid containing 40 wt% water is dried until it contains 10 wt% water. How much water is removed?
questions.why: The 60 kg of dry solid is 90% of the product, so the product is 66.7 kg and 33.3 kg of water is removed. 30.0 kg assumes the water percentage falls by 30 points of the original 100 kg, ignoring that the product is lighter than the feed. 34.0 kg takes the remaining water as 10% of the dry solid (6 kg) rather than 10% of the wet product. 40.0 kg is all the water, but the product still holds about 6.7 kg.

questions.q: A distillation column is fed 100 kmol/h of a benzene–toluene mixture containing 40 mol% benzene. The distillate contains 95 mol% benzene and the bottoms 5 mol% benzene. Find the distillate and bottoms flows and the fractional recovery of benzene in the distillate.
markScheme: Total balance F = D + B (1 mark)
Benzene balance 40 = 0.95D + 0.05B (1 mark)
D = 38.9 kmol/h (1 mark)
B = 61.1 kmol/h (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Total: 100 = D + B. Benzene: 0.40 × 100 = 0.95D + 0.05B. Substituting B = 100 − D gives 40 = 0.90D + 5, so D = 38.9 kmol/h and B = 61.1 kmol/h. Benzene in distillate = 0.95 × 38.9 = 36.9 kmol/h, so the fractional recovery is 36.9/40 = 0.924 (92.4%). Check toluene: in 60; out 0.05 × 38.9 + 0.95 × 61.1 = 1.9 + 58.1 = 60.0 kmol/h.

questions.q: Fresh feed of 100 mol/h of pure A enters a process. The reactor achieves 25% single-pass conversion of A, and a perfect separator recycles all unreacted A. What is the recycle flow?
questions.why: Overall, all 100 mol/h of A reacts, so the reactor feed must satisfy 0.25 × feed = 100, giving 400 mol/h, of which 300 mol/h is recycle. 400 mol/h is the total reactor feed, not the recycle. 75 mol/h is only the unreacted part of the fresh feed after one pass; it ignores that recycled A also passes through and only 25% of it reacts each time. 33.3 mol/h comes from swapping the conversion and the unreacted fraction: taking the reactor feed as 100/0.75 = 133 mol/h leaves 33.3 mol/h as recycle.

questions.q: Why is a purge stream added to a recycle loop?
options: To stop inert components in the feed from accumulating in the loop
To increase the single-pass conversion in the reactor
To remove the main product from the process
To reduce the amount of fresh feed needed for a given production rate
questions.why: Without a purge, an inert that the separator cannot remove has no exit, so at steady state its inventory would grow without limit. Single-pass conversion is set by the reactor, not the purge. The product is removed by the separator, not the purge. A purge actually increases the fresh feed needed, because some reactant is lost with the purged gas.

questions.q: A stream of 100 mol/h contains 5 mol% impurity. A clean-up unit removes all of the impurity from whatever passes through it (the removed stream is pure impurity). Some of the feed bypasses the unit so that the remixed product contains exactly 1 mol% impurity. Find the fraction of feed that bypasses and the product flow.
markScheme: Bypass fraction f defined; impurity in product = 5f mol/h (1 mark)
Product flow = 100 − 5(1 − f) mol/h (1 mark)
Specification 5f/(95 + 5f) = 0.01 set up (1 mark)
Product ≈ 96.0 mol/h (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Let a fraction f bypass. The 100(1 − f) mol/h through the unit loses its impurity, 5(1 − f) mol/h. Product = 100 − 5(1 − f) = 95 + 5f mol/h, containing the bypassed impurity 5f mol/h. Specification: 5f/(95 + 5f) = 0.01, so 5f = 0.95 + 0.05f, 4.95f = 0.95 and f = 0.192. Product = 95 + 5 × 0.192 = 96.0 mol/h (impurity 0.96 mol/h, which is 1.0 mol%).

questions.q: A reactor is fed 100 mol N₂ and 250 mol H₂ for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Which statement is correct?
options: H₂ is limiting and N₂ is in 20% excess
H₂ is limiting and N₂ is in 16.7% excess
N₂ is limiting and H₂ is in 150% excess
The feed is in the stoichiometric ratio
questions.why: H₂ gives 250/3 = 83.3 per unit coefficient and N₂ gives 100, so H₂ runs out first. N₂ needed = 83.3 mol, so the excess is (100 − 83.3)/83.3 = 20%. 16.7% divides the surplus by the amount fed instead of by the stoichiometric requirement. Calling N₂ limiting with 150% excess H₂ compares raw moles (250 vs 100) without the 3:1 coefficient ratio. The stoichiometric ratio would need 300 mol H₂, not 250.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, a reactor fed with no ammonia produces 40 mol of NH₃. What is the extent of reaction?
questions.why: n_NH₃ = 0 + 2ξ, so ξ = 40/2 = 20 mol. 40 mol ignores the coefficient of 2 on ammonia. 80 mol multiplies by the coefficient instead of dividing. 13.3 mol divides by 3, the coefficient of hydrogen, which is the wrong species for this balance.

questions.q: Ethylene is oxidised: C₂H₄ + ½O₂ → C₂H₄O (desired) and C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O (undesired). For 100 mol C₂H₄ fed, the outlet contains 20 mol C₂H₄ and 56 mol C₂H₄O. Find the conversion of ethylene, the CO₂ formed, the yield of ethylene oxide based on ethylene consumed, and the selectivity (ethylene oxide formed per ethylene burned).
markScheme: Ethylene consumed = 80 mol, conversion 0.80 (1 mark)
Extents: ξ₁ = 56 mol, ξ₂ = 24 mol (1 mark)
CO₂ formed = 2ξ₂ = 48 mol (1 mark)
Yield on consumption = 56/80 = 0.70 (1 mark)
Selectivity = 56/24 = 2.33 (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Ethylene consumed = 100 − 20 = 80 mol, so conversion = 80/100 = 0.80. The desired reaction has extent ξ₁ = 56 mol (one ethylene oxide per extent). The rest of the consumed ethylene burns: ξ₂ = 80 − 56 = 24 mol, forming 2 × 24 = 48 mol CO₂ (and 48 mol H₂O). Yield based on ethylene consumed = 56/80 = 0.70. Selectivity = 56/24 = 2.33 mol of ethylene oxide per mol of ethylene burned.

questions.q: 100 mol/h of methane is burned with 20% excess air (21 mol% O₂). What is the air flow?
questions.why: Theoretical O₂ is 200 mol/h, so 240 mol/h of O₂ is fed and the air is 240/0.21 = 1143 mol/h. 240 mol/h is the oxygen, not the air. 952 mol/h is the theoretical air (200/0.21) with no excess. 1371 mol/h applies the 20% excess twice (1.2 × 240/0.21).

questions.q: For complete combustion of methane with 20% excess air, what is the mole percentage of CO₂ in the flue gas on a dry basis?
questions.why: Per 100 mol CH₄ the dry flue gas holds 100 CO₂, 40 O₂ and 903 N₂, a total of 1043 mol, so CO₂ = 9.6%. 8.0% is the wet-basis value, which includes 200 mol of water. 11.7% is the dry figure for stoichiometric air (100 CO₂ with 752 N₂), so it ignores the excess. 33.3% is CO₂ as a fraction of CO₂ plus water only, leaving out nitrogen and oxygen.

questions.q: Propane (C₃H₈) is burned completely with 25% excess air. Per mole of propane, find the air fed and the composition of the wet flue gas, and give the mole fraction of water in it.
markScheme: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, theoretical O₂ = 5 mol (1 mark)
O₂ fed = 6.25 mol; air = 6.25/0.21 = 29.8 mol (1 mark)
N₂ = 23.5 mol; excess O₂ = 1.25 mol (1 mark)
Products: CO₂ 3, H₂O 4, O₂ 1.25, N₂ 23.5; total 31.8 mol (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, so theoretical O₂ = 5 mol per mol propane. With 25% excess, O₂ fed = 6.25 mol and air = 6.25/0.21 = 29.8 mol, bringing 0.79 × 29.8 = 23.5 mol N₂. Flue gas per mol propane: CO₂ 3, H₂O 4, O₂ 6.25 − 5 = 1.25, N₂ 23.5; total 31.8 mol. Mole fraction of water = 4/31.8 = 0.126.

questions.q: 2 kg/s of water (c_p ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg K) is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C by condensing saturated steam with a latent heat of 2200 kJ/kg. Neglecting losses, what steam flow is needed?
questions.why: Q̇ = 2 × 4.18 × 50 = 418 kW, and steam = 418/2200 = 0.19 kg/s. 0.27 kg/s uses the outlet temperature (70) in place of the temperature rise (50). 0.045 kg/s leaves out the heat capacity, multiplying mass flow by ΔT only. 5.3 kg/s divides the latent heat by the duty, inverting the ratio.

questions.q: Which of the following is a state function?
questions.why: Enthalpy depends only on the state of the material (temperature, pressure, phase, composition), so its change is independent of path. Heat and shaft work are energy in transit and their amounts depend on the route between two states. Frictional dissipation also depends on how the process is carried out, so it is not a property of the state.

questions.q: 1000 kg/h of liquid water is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C in a heat exchanger by saturated steam, which leaves as saturated condensate. Taking c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg K and the latent heat as 2200 kJ/kg, find the heat duty and the steam flow. State your assumptions.
markScheme: Steady-flow energy balance with ΔE_k, ΔE_p and shaft work neglected; no heat losses (1 mark)
Q̇ = ṁc_pΔT with ṁ in kg/s (1 mark)
Q̇ = 69.7 kW (1 mark)
Steam flow = Q̇/λ (1 mark)
Steam ≈ 0.0317 kg/s ≈ 114 kg/h (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Assume steady state, no heat loss to the surroundings, no shaft work and negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy, so Q̇ = ΔḢ for each side. Water: ṁ = 1000/3600 = 0.278 kg/s; Q̇ = 0.278 × 4.18 × (80 − 20) = 69.7 kW. The steam gives up only its latent heat, so ṁ_steam = 69.7/2200 = 0.0317 kg/s = 114 kg/h.

questions.q: Using ΔĤ_f° values (kJ/mol) CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(g) −241.8 and H₂O(l) −285.8, what is ΔĤ_r° for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g)?
questions.why: ΔĤ_r° = −393.5 + 2(−241.8) − (−74.8) = −802.3 kJ/mol. −890.3 kJ/mol uses liquid water, but the question specifies vapour. −560.5 kJ/mol counts only one mole of water instead of two. −951.9 kJ/mol adds the heat of formation of methane instead of subtracting it as a reactant.

questions.q: Why is the higher heating value of a fuel larger than its lower heating value?
options: The higher heating value assumes the water produced is condensed, recovering its latent heat
The lower heating value assumes the water produced is liquid
The higher heating value includes heat from oxidising the nitrogen in the air
The two differ only because they use different reference temperatures
questions.why: Condensing the product water releases its latent heat, so a basis with liquid water gives a larger heat release. The lower heating value is the one with water as vapour, so saying it assumes liquid water reverses the definitions. Nitrogen is treated as inert in heating values. Both values are normally quoted at the same reference temperature; the difference is the phase of the water.

questions.q: 10 mol/s of methane is burned completely in air. Feed and products are both at 25 °C and water leaves as vapour. Using ΔĤ_r° = −802.3 kJ/mol CH₄, find the heat that must be removed and explain the sign.
markScheme: Energy balance reduces to Q̇ = ΔḢ = ξΔĤ_r° because inlet and outlet are at the reference temperature (1 mark)
ξ = 10 mol/s (1 mark)
Negative Q̇ means heat leaves the system (exothermic reaction) (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: With inlet and outlet at 25 °C, all sensible enthalpy terms are zero relative to the standard state, so Q̇ = ΔḢ = ξΔĤ_r°. Complete combustion of 10 mol/s gives ξ = 10 mol/s, so Q̇ = 10 × (−802.3) = −8023 kW. The negative sign means heat flows out of the system: about 8.0 MW must be removed to hold the products at 25 °C (strictly, water would partly condense at 25 °C; the vapour basis is an assumption of the question).

questions.q:
A fresh feed of 100 mol/h containing 99 mol% A and 1 mol% inert I is mixed with a recycle stream and fed to a reactor where A → B with 20% single-pass conversion of A. The reactor outlet goes to a separator that removes all the B as product. The remaining stream (unreacted A and all the I) is split: part is recycled and part is purged. The I content of the purge is limited to 10 mol%.
(a) Draw and label the flowsheet and carry out a degree-of-freedom analysis for the overall process. [5]
(b) Find the purge flow and the overall conversion of A. [5]
(c) Find the reactor feed and the recycle flow. [6]
(d) Explain qualitatively what would happen to the recycle flow and to the overall conversion if the allowed I content of the purge were raised to 20 mol%. [4]
markScheme: Correct labelled flowsheet with mixer, reactor, separator and splitter; splitter outlets share the same composition (2 marks)
Overall DOF: unknowns P, n_B and extent ξ against balances on A, B and I gives DOF = 0 (3 marks)
I balance: 1 = 0.10P so P = 10 mol/h; A in purge = 9 mol/h (2 marks)
A reacted = 99 − 9 = 90 mol/h; overall conversion = 90/99 = 0.909 (3 marks)
Reactor A feed = 90/0.20 = 450 mol/h; A leaving reactor = 360 mol/h (2 marks)
Splitter inlet = 360/0.9 = 400 mol/h, recycle = 390 mol/h (3 marks)
Mixer check: 99 + 0.9 × 390 = 450 mol/h A; I: 1 + 0.1 × 390 = 40 mol/h (1 mark)
Part (d): purge flow halves (5 mol/h), less A lost, overall conversion rises (to 95/99 ≈ 0.96); I builds up to a higher level in the loop so recycle flow rises (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Flowsheet: fresh feed (100 mol/h; 0.99 A, 0.01 I) → mixer ← recycle R (A, I). Mixer outlet → reactor (A → B, 20% single-pass conversion) → separator → product (pure B) and a stream of A + I → splitter → recycle R and purge P. Both splitter outlets have the same composition, 0.90 A and 0.10 I.
Overall boundary: streams crossing it are fresh feed (known), product B (unknown n_B) and purge P (unknown flow, known composition). Unknowns: P, n_B and the extent ξ. Equations: balances on A, B and I (3). DOF = 3 − 3 = 0, so the overall balance can be solved first.

(b) I is inert and leaves only in the purge: 1 = 0.10P, so P = 10 mol/h. A in purge = 0.90 × 10 = 9 mol/h. Overall A: 99 = ξ + 9, so ξ = 90 mol/h of A reacts (and 90 mol/h of B is produced). Overall conversion of A = 90/99 = 0.909 (90.9%).

(c) Reactor: 20% of the A entering reacts and the reaction rate is the same 90 mol/h, so A entering = 90/0.20 = 450 mol/h and A leaving = 450 − 90 = 360 mol/h. All of this A goes to the splitter in a stream that is 90% A, so splitter inlet = 360/0.90 = 400 mol/h (360 A + 40 I). Recycle R = 400 − 10 = 390 mol/h (351 A, 39 I).
Check at the mixer: A = 99 + 351 = 450 mol/h; I = 1 + 39 = 40 mol/h. The reactor feed is 490 mol/h with about 8.2 mol% I.

(d) With a 20 mol% limit, P = 1/0.20 = 5 mol/h, containing only 4 mol/h of A, so the reactant lost falls and the overall conversion rises to 95/99 ≈ 0.96. However, the loop now runs with more inert: the reactor still converts 20% per pass, so A entering = 95/0.2 = 475 mol/h and A leaving = 380 mol/h; splitter inlet = 380/0.8 = 475 mol/h and recycle = 470 mol/h, larger than before. The trade-off is lower raw-material loss against a larger recycle (bigger equipment and compression or pumping costs) and a more dilute reactor feed.

questions.q:
Methane is burned completely with 20% excess air (21 mol% O₂, 79 mol% N₂). Fuel and air enter at 25 °C.
(a) Per mole of methane, find the moles of each species in the flue gas and give the flue gas composition on a dry basis. [7]
(b) Using ΔĤ_r° = −802.3 kJ/mol (water as vapour) and mean heat capacities over the range (J/mol K): CO₂ 54, H₂O(g) 43, O₂ 35, N₂ 33, estimate the adiabatic flame temperature. [8]
(c) Explain why the real adiabatic flame temperature is lower than your estimate, and how increasing the excess air would change it. [5]
markScheme: Theoretical O₂ = 2 mol; O₂ fed = 2.4 mol; N₂ = 2.4 × 79/21 = 9.03 mol (2 marks)
Flue gas: CO₂ 1, H₂O 2, O₂ 0.4, N₂ 9.03 mol (2 marks)
Dry total 10.43 mol; dry composition CO₂ 9.6%, O₂ 3.8%, N₂ 86.6% (3 marks)
Adiabatic energy balance: heat released = Σ n c̄_p (T_ad − 25) with reference 25 °C (2 marks)
Σ n c̄_p = 54 + 86 + 14 + 298 = 452 J/K per mol CH₄ (2 marks)
Real value lower: dissociation (endothermic) at high T and c_p rising with T; any heat losses (3 marks)
More excess air lowers T_ad because the same heat is spread over more gas (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Theoretical O₂ = 2 mol per mol CH₄; with 20% excess, O₂ fed = 2.4 mol and N₂ = 2.4 × (79/21) = 9.03 mol (air = 11.43 mol).
Flue gas per mol CH₄: CO₂ = 1; H₂O = 2; O₂ = 2.4 − 2 = 0.4; N₂ = 9.03. Wet total = 12.43 mol.
Dry total = 1 + 0.4 + 9.03 = 10.43 mol. Dry composition: CO₂ = 1/10.43 = 9.6%; O₂ = 0.4/10.43 = 3.8%; N₂ = 9.03/10.43 = 86.6%.

(b) Take reactants and products at 25 °C as the reference (heat of reaction method). For an adiabatic burner with no work, ΔḢ = 0:
ξΔĤ_r° + Σ n_i c̄_p,i (T_ad − 25) = 0, with ξ = 1 mol.
Σ n_i c̄_p,i = 1(54) + 2(43) + 0.4(35) + 9.03(33) = 54 + 86 + 14 + 297.9 = 451.9 J/K.
T_ad − 25 = 802 300/451.9 = 1775 K, so T_ad ≈ 1800 °C.
(For comparison, the same data with stoichiometric air, 7.52 mol N₂ and no excess O₂, give Σ n c̄_p = 388 J/K and T_ad ≈ 2090 °C.)

(c) The estimate is too high because: (i) at flame temperatures CO₂ and H₂O partly dissociate (to CO, H₂, O₂, OH and others), which is endothermic and absorbs some of the heat; (ii) real heat capacities increase with temperature, so a single mean value from a lower range understates the heat needed; (iii) real burners lose heat by radiation and convection. For reference, the adiabatic flame temperature of methane in stoichiometric air is about 1950 °C (approximate). Increasing the excess air adds more N₂ and O₂ that must be heated by the same heat release, so T_ad falls; too little air instead leaves unburnt fuel and CO, also lowering the temperature and wasting fuel.
